issues.legal_issue: The evidence established that the eyewitnesses had sufficient light and opportunity to identify the offenders despite the alleged interruption in electricity supply.
material_facts: A defence witness produced a register indicating an interruption in electricity supply, but he had not made or certified the relevant entry.
The register was unbound and did not specify the areas receiving electricity; neither the operator who made the entry nor the officer said to have certified it testified.
The informant said he was watching television when the offenders entered, and other witnesses testified that there was electricity during the occurrence.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the defence evidence as insufficient to establish that there was no electricity at the time and accepted that the witnesses had sufficient light and opportunity to identify the offenders.
issues.legal_principle: The evidence about lighting must be assessed as a whole. The Court relied on the limitations in the register and the testimony of the witnesses, including the informant’s account that he was watching television; it cited no separate statute or earlier case for this determination.

rule.if: appeal_from_conviction and informant_watched_tv_during_occurrence and eyewitnesses_reported_usable_light and register_author_and_certifier_not_examined and register_did_not_specify_affected_area

predicates.appeal_from_conviction: The accused appealed a conviction arising from a criminal trial.
predicates.informant_watched_tv_during_occurrence: The informant said that he was watching television when the offence occurred.
predicates.eyewitnesses_reported_usable_light: Eyewitnesses said that there was enough light to see the offenders.
predicates.register_author_and_certifier_not_examin: The person who made the electricity-register entry and the person said to have certified it did not testify.
predicates.register_did_not_specify_affected_area: The electricity register did not identify the areas to which its recorded supply information applied.

issues.definition: When an appeal from a conviction involves an informant who watched television during the occurrence, eyewitnesses who reported usable light, and an unauthenticated register that did not specify the affected area, the witnesses had sufficient light to identify the offenders.

issues.legal_issue: A sole eyewitness’s identification, corroborated by a test identification parade held about a month after the offence, may reliably sustain a conviction when the circumstances support the witness’s ability to identify the accused.
material_facts: The eyewitness lived with the informant’s family, was present during the dacoity, suffered five injuries, and was involved in resisting the offenders at close quarters.
The occurrence lasted about 25 minutes, and the witness said there was electric light.
The witness identified the accused in court and in a test identification parade held about a month after the occurrence.
Before the parade, the witness had described the accused’s attempt to assault him; that account was recorded by the Magistrate conducting the parade.

The defence did not allege that the accused had been shown to the witness beforehand or that the parade was irregular, and the testimony of the Magistrate and investigating officer on the parade was not challenged.
issues.conclusion: The Court found the witness reliable and his in-court identification corroborated by the parade. The delay and the fact that he was the sole identifying witness did not make the identification unsafe; the appeal was dismissed and the conviction stood.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 9 of the Evidence Act, facts establishing identity are relevant. In-court identification is substantive evidence, while a prior test identification parade is investigative and serves to test and strengthen its trustworthiness; under Section 162 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the parade does not itself constitute substantive evidence. A parade is not legally required, and identification evidence may be accepted without corroboration where the court finds the witness reliable. There is no invariable rule fixing the permissible interval before a parade or requiring a particular number of identifying witnesses: the court assesses the evidence and circumstances in each case. The Court relied on Malkhansingh v. State of Madhya Pradesh, Anil Kumar v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Bharat Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh, among other cited decisions, and distinguished Wakil Singh v. State of Bihar, Subhash and Shiv Shankar v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Soni v. State of Uttar Pradesh on their facts.

predicates.appeal_from_conviction: The accused appealed a conviction arising from a criminal trial.
predicates.sole_identifying_witness_had_close_obser: The sole identifying witness encountered the offender at close quarters while the offence was occurring.
predicates.witness_suffered_injuries_during_occurre: The identifying witness was injured during the occurrence while resisting or defending against the offenders.
predicates.occurrence_allowed_extended_observation: The occurrence lasted long enough to give the witness an opportunity to observe the offenders beyond a fleeting glimpse.
predicates.witness_identified_accused_in_court_and_: The witness identified the accused both in court and in a prior identification parade.
predicates.parade_identification_was_not_shown_irre: The defence did not establish that the identification parade was conducted irregularly.
predicates.no_prior_exposure_was_alleged: The defence did not allege that the accused had been shown to the witness before the identification parade.

issues.definition: When an appeal from a conviction involves a sole identifying witness who had close and extended observation, was injured during the occurrence, identified the accused in court and at a parade, and faced no substantiated claim of parade irregularity or prior exposure, the identification evidence was reliable to sustain the conviction.
